note: Wine builtin modules added to the 64-bit (ARM64EC) DLL farm, app/Madeira/arm64ec-windows, by build/wine-pe/build-arm64ec-farm.sh. The farm grew by hand (143 files) while the 32-bit farm takes every module (build/wine-i386/build.sh); a 64-bit program that imports a module not here stops at 'Library X (which is needed by ...) not found'. Every arm64ec module is mapped straight from its file, so FileAlignment is 0x10000 and the smallest module is about 0.5 MiB: the whole Wine set would be about 500 MiB, so modules are added by group, each with the reason it is needed. The groups follow the Windows components Winlator installs on demand (its assets/wincomponents/wincomponents.json: direct3d, directsound, directmusic, directshow, directplay, xaudio, vcrun2005, vcrun2010, wmdecoder), which are Microsoft's redistributable DLLs there; here the same names are answered by Wine's own implementations, built from the wine submodule, never by Microsoft binaries. Modules already in the farm are not rebuilt unless --refresh is given, so device-tested binaries stay as they are. DirectMusic is not in the 64-bit farm: Windows itself never shipped 64-bit DirectMusic (Winlator's directmusic component installs into syswow64 only), so only 32-bit programs use it, and the 32-bit farm has it.

groups.name: directshow
groups.reason: DirectShow playback (intro videos, FMV): quartz is the filter graph every DirectShow player creates (CLSID_FilterGraph); the prefix registry already names these classes, the DLLs were missing for 64-bit programs. Decoding goes through winegstreamer (see media_foundation). avicap32 is here because devenum imports it to list video capture devices; its unix side (V4L) does not exist on iOS, so the list is empty, which is the answer a machine without a camera gives.

groups.name: media_foundation
groups.reason: Media Foundation playback, the path Unity, Unreal and most 2015+ games use for intro and in-game video (IMFMediaEngine, IMFPMediaPlayer, the source resolver). mf, mfplat and mfreadwrite were in the farm without the media engine, the sources, the EVR presenter and the decoder MFTs they load, so playback failed at the first object a game asked for. winegstreamer's PE half is upstream's; its 64-bit unix side stays behind MADEIRA_WG_64BIT=1 (docs/MEDIA.md), so without that switch these objects load and report the decoder as unavailable, which is how Wine without GStreamer behaves and what games are written to handle. Wine 11's own byte-stream sources (mfsrcsnk, mfasfsrcsnk, mfmp4srcsnk) are left out: they demux through winedmo, whose unix side is FFmpeg on the host and has no iOS port yet, so they could only fail; the source resolver then uses winegstreamer's handler, whose unix side this port does have.

groups.name: wmdecoder
groups.reason: Windows Media format: WMV/WMA playback through the Windows Media Format SDK (wmvcore's WMCreateSyncReader / WMCreateReader) and the WMA decoder DMO FAudio asks COM for when a game plays xWMA.

groups.name: vfw_acm_mci
groups.reason: Video for Windows, ACM codecs and MCI: AVI cutscenes (avifil32/msvfw32 with the Cinepak, RLE and Video 1 decoders), compressed WAV (IMA/MS ADPCM, GSM, G.711, MP3 through l3codeca) and the ACM wave mapper driver (msacm32.drv) that winmm needs to convert a format the device does not take; mciavi32/mciwave/mciseq/midimap answer mciSendString and MIDI music.

groups.name: xaudio
groups.reason: XAudio2, X3DAudio, XAPOFX and XACT, every version a DirectX SDK shipped. Only x3daudio1_7 and xapofx1_5 were in the 64-bit farm, so a game linked against xaudio2_7 (the June 2010 SDK, the most common) or xaudio2_9 (Windows 10) could not start. Wine builds them from one source with FAudio bundled (libs/faudio), output through mmdevapi like the rest of the audio. XACT2 (xactengine2_*) is left out: it belongs to 2006-2007 SDKs whose games are 32-bit, and the 32-bit farm has it.

groups.name: directplay
groups.reason: DirectPlay: games that create the DirectPlay8 or legacy DirectPlay objects at start-up, even for single player, stop when the class is missing. The dplaysvr/dpnsvr helper programs are not included (no 64-bit Wine program is shipped yet).

groups.name: direct3d_helpers
groups.reason: The D3DX and HLSL compiler libraries of every DirectX SDK. Only d3dx9_43, d3dcompiler_43 and d3dcompiler_47 were in the 64-bit farm, so a game built against an earlier SDK (d3dx9_24..42, d3dx10_*, d3dx11_*) stopped at its first import. Wine's d3dx and d3dcompiler are CPU-side libraries over vkd3d-shader (bundled in libs/vkd3d, no Vulkan involved) and do not touch the renderer. d3dx9_24..30 (the 2004-2006 SDKs) are left out of the 64-bit farm: the 32-bit farm has them, and 64-bit games of that period are too rare to justify 10 MiB.

groups.name: direct3d10_frontends
groups.reason: Direct3D 10 entry points. DXMT answers d3d10core.dll (D3D10CoreCreateDevice) but neither d3d10.dll nor d3d10_1.dll, which is where a Direct3D 10 game calls D3D10CreateDevice(AndSwapChain)(1); Wine's two DLLs are thin frontends that create the device through d3d10core, the same arrangement DXVK uses since 2.0, so DXMT renders the frames. d2d1 (Direct2D, used by launchers and game UIs) creates its device the same way, through d3d10_1/d3d11. ddraw is imported by dxdiagn and amstream. It is Wine's DirectDraw over wined3d, which has no OpenGL or Vulkan backend in this port (the same state as the 64-bit Wine d3d9.dll already in the farm): the import resolves and DirectDraw objects are created, but whether a 64-bit DirectDraw program draws anything is unproven and needs an iPad test. 64-bit DirectDraw games are rare; the 32-bit farm ships ddraw already.

groups.name: vcrun_legacy
groups.reason: Visual C++ runtimes older than 2015. Only msvcr120 and the 2015-2022 set were in the 64-bit farm; a 64-bit game built with Visual Studio 2005-2012 imports msvcr80/90/100/110 and msvcp80/90/100/110 (plus vcomp for OpenMP and atl for COM), and stopped at load. Wine's msvcr*/msvcp* are complete C/C++ runtimes built from one source (dlls/msvcrt, dlls/msvcp90). msvcr70/71 and msvcp70/71 are left out: Visual Studio .NET 2002/2003 had no 64-bit compiler, so no 64-bit program imports them (the 32-bit farm has them).

groups.name: game_system_libs
groups.reason: System libraries games and their launchers import directly and that the 64-bit farm lacked: GDI+ (launcher and UI images), Uniscribe and rich edit (text in launchers and dialogs), MSXML (settings files), WMI (wbemprox: engines query Win32_VideoController for the adapter and its memory), the game explorer (gameux), error reporting (wer/faultrep, imported by Unreal and Unity crash handlers), cabinet/xmllite/mscms (pulled in by setup code and WIC), and the typelibs OLE automation loads.

groups.name: delay_import_closure
groups.reason: Delay-import targets of modules already in the farm that were missing from it: gdiplus/shlwapi -> mlang, advapi32 -> cryptsp, urlmon -> advpack, shell32 -> shdocvw, bthprops -> bluetoothapis. A missing delay-load target is not caught at load time; the first call aborts with an unimplemented-function crash (seen in testing for wmvcore -> winegstreamer). opengl32 -> glu32 is left out: GL is a stub on iOS.

groups.name: side_by_side
groups.reason: Common Controls 6.0 for 64-bit programs. A program whose manifest asks for Microsoft.Windows.Common-Controls 6.0 (most Windows programs and many game launchers, crash reporters and setup tools do) gets it from C:\windows\winsxs, which Madeira seeds at launch from the session's farm (app/Madeira/WinSxS.c). comctl32_v6 is that assembly's comctl32.dll; without it the 64-bit store had no Common Controls 6, the program got comctl32 5.x, and its TaskDialog / TaskDialogIndirect imports were bound to stubs that abort when called (build/host-tests/check-winsxs.py shows this under Wine). The VC80/VC90 CRT and ATL, GDI+ and MSXML 3/6 assemblies are backed by modules already in the farm. msxml4 (Msxml2 4.0) is added by the installer_scripting group, which has the evidence for it.

groups.name: installer_scripting
groups.reason: Windows Installer, script hosts and the COM servers the 64-bit prefix already registers without a DLL behind them (counted from the template's system.reg: msxml4 11 classes, hnetcfg 8, wshom.ocx 5, msxml/msxml2 5 each, vbscript 4, msi/scrrun/jscript/wbemdisp 3 each). A 64-bit redistributable or game installer (vcredist_x64, PhysX, a game's own .msi), and an x64 custom action, run in msi.dll / msiexec.exe from system32: the 64-bit farm had neither, so the compat catalogue's 'msi: builtin' was true of 32-bit programs only. Launchers and setup scripts create Scripting.FileSystemObject (scrrun), WScript.Shell (wshom.ocx), the JScript / VBScript engines and SWbemLocator (wbemdisp); multiplayer games open the Windows Firewall API (HNetCfg.FwMgr, hnetcfg) to add their exception and treat a class that does not load as a fatal setup error. msxml4 completes the side-by-side store (Msxml2 4.0 was the one assembly WinSxS.c could not seed for 64-bit) and backs MSXML2.DOMDocument.4.0; msxml / msxml2 are the older ProgIDs' servers. sensapi (IsNetworkAlive) and shfolder (SHGetFolderPath) are plain imports of games and their network libraries. jscript / vbscript exist in the aarch64 farm, which only native ARM64 processes can load. About 11 MiB in all; mshtml / ieframe (36 + 11 classes) stay out: they need wine-gecko, which is not shipped. mspatcha (patch application) and odbccp32 (SQLInstallDriverEx for ODBC install actions) are msi.dll imports: the build refuses msi without them.
